topic.subject: maths
topic.title: Integers
topic.scope: negative numbers, number line, ordering, addition, subtraction, multiplication and division of integers

nodes.name: Addition and Subtraction
external_prereqs: addition and subtraction of whole numbers

nodes.name: Further from zero means smaller for negatives
Subtracting negative is same as subtracting positive
Product of two negatives is negative

misconceptions.statement: -5 is smaller than -10 because 5 is smaller than 10.
misconceptions.why: Students apply whole number magnitude rules to negative integers.
misconceptions.fix: On the number line, numbers to the right are always greater; -5 is to the right of -10.
misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: Adding a negative number always makes the total smaller.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the operation of addition with the property of the negative sign.
misconceptions.fix: Adding a negative number is equivalent to subtracting its positive counterpart.
misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: The product of two negative numbers is negative.
misconceptions.why: Students assume the negative sign 'wins' or persists in the result.
misconceptions.fix: The product of two negative numbers is always positive.
misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: Subtracting a negative number is the same as subtracting a positive.
misconceptions.why: Students ignore the double negative sign and treat it as a single subtraction.
misconceptions.fix: Subtracting a negative number is the same as adding a positive number.
misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: When adding a positive and a negative number, you always give the answer the sign of the first number.
misconceptions.why: Students learn a surface rule 'keep the first sign' and ignore which number has the greater absolute value.
misconceptions.fix: For unlike signs, subtract the smaller absolute value from the larger and take the sign of the number with the larger absolute value. E.g. 3 + (-7) = -4.
misconceptions.root_belief: Answer takes sign of the first number

misconceptions.statement: When adding two negative numbers, the negatives cancel and the answer is positive.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the rule for multiplying two negatives with the rule for adding them.
misconceptions.fix: Adding two negative numbers means moving further left on the number line, so the sum is negative. E.g. (-3) + (-4) = -7.
misconceptions.root_belief: Two negatives always make a positive

misconceptions.statement: Subtraction is commutative, so 3 - 8 gives the same answer as 8 - 3.
misconceptions.why: Students think of subtraction as 'the bigger minus the smaller' and drop the sign when the result is below zero.
misconceptions.root_belief: Smaller minus bigger is the same as reversed
misconceptions.source_hint: research on whole-number bias in integer subtraction

misconceptions.statement: Any negative number is greater than 0 or at least equal to it, as 0 means nothing.
misconceptions.why: Students link negative numbers with 'nothing' and think zero is the lowest possible value.
misconceptions.fix: Zero is greater than every negative number, because negatives lie to the left of 0 on the number line.
misconceptions.root_belief: Zero is the smallest possible number

misconceptions.statement: The minus sign in -5 only means 'subtract' and does not tell us that the number itself is negative.
misconceptions.why: Students only know the minus sign as an operation from whole-number arithmetic.
misconceptions.fix: The minus sign can show an operation (7 - 5) or the sign of a number (-5, five units left of zero). Position tells which one.

probe.question: What does the sign in 'x = -5' mean? How is it read?
probe.wrong_answer: It means subtract 5 from something, so there is nothing to read as a number.

misconceptions.root_belief: Minus sign always indicates the operation subtraction
misconceptions.source_hint: research on dual meaning of the minus sign

misconceptions.statement: The product of a negative and a positive number is positive when the positive number is larger.
misconceptions.why: Students base the sign on which number is bigger instead of how many factors are negative.
misconceptions.fix: A positive times a negative is always negative. E.g. 8 × (-2) = -16.
misconceptions.root_belief: Bigger number decides the sign of the product

misconceptions.statement: When a negative number is divided by a positive number, the answer is positive because division reduces the number.
misconceptions.why: Students think division only 'shares out' and cannot make the answer negative; they apply sign rules without meaning.
misconceptions.fix: Dividing integers with unlike signs gives a negative quotient. E.g. (-12) ÷ 3 = -4, since 3 × (-4) = -12.
misconceptions.root_belief: Division always gives a positive result

misconceptions.statement: A negative number cannot show a real-life quantity, since you cannot have less than nothing.
misconceptions.why: Students link numbers only to counting objects, so they cannot read a loss, debt or fall as an opposite direction.
misconceptions.fix: Integers show opposite situations: profit and loss, rise and fall, above and below sea level, using positive and negative numbers.

probe.question: A diver is 15 m below sea level. How can this be written as an integer?
probe.wrong_answer: It cannot be written, only 15 m

misconceptions.root_belief: Numbers only count real objects present
misconceptions.source_hint: research on historical and student resistance to negatives
